title: The Hanseatic League
text:
In the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, German merchants trading across the North Sea and the Baltic faced pirates, unpredictable foreign rulers and little protection from their own distant emperor. They responded by banding together. Merchants from the same towns traveled in groups, and in foreign trading centers they formed associations, or hansas, to defend their rights.

Over time the towns themselves cooperated. Led by Lubeck, dozens of cities, including Hamburg, Bremen, Cologne, Danzig, Riga and Visby, formed a loose league. Its merchants ran trading posts in London, Bruges, Bergen and Novgorod, where they lived under their own rules. From the fourteenth century, delegates of the member towns met in a general assembly, the Hanseatic Diet, usually in Lubeck.

The league had no permanent army, no common treasury and few officials. Its chief weapon was collective action. If a ruler or a city broke its agreements, the league could impose a trade embargo, and a member town that refused to cooperate could be expelled. When King Valdemar IV of Denmark captured Visby and threatened the league's trade, the towns allied, went to war, and in the Treaty of Stralsund of 1370 forced Denmark to grant them trading privileges and control of fortresses on the Danish coast for fifteen years.

The league declined from the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, as strong territorial states and new trade routes arose. Its last diet met in 1669. Hamburg, Bremen and Lubeck still call themselves Hanseatic cities.
lesson: Independent members can achieve great power by acting together under shared rules. A credible commitment to collective action can replace an army.
people: Merchants and towns of the Hanseatic League, Valdemar IV of Denmark
location: North Sea and Baltic coasts (Germany, Poland, the Baltic states, Sweden and beyond)
source: Philippe Dollinger, The German Hansa (1964; English translation 1970)
